title: Managing Unit Cost with Vendor Rebates - Accrued vs Realized Impact

posts.name: Eabellom
posts.cooked:
Hi ERPNext Community,

I need help managing the following vendor rebate scenario and its impact on unit costing:

SCENARIO:

  • Purchase 100 units for $1,000 ($10/unit from supplier)
  • Have an agreed volume rebate of $100 (to be realized later through cross-invoicing)
  • Expected final cost: $900 ($9/unit)

COSTING CHALLENGE:
The rebate impacts unit cost in two phases:

  1. Accrued Phase: Rebate is promised but not yet realized

    • Should unit cost reflect expected $9/unit or current $10/unit?
    • How to handle “expected cost” vs “actual cost” in inventory valuation?

  2. Realized Phase: When rebate is executed (supplier invoices us $100 for marketing services)

    • Need to adjust unit cost retroactively to $9/unit
    • Impact on weighted average cost and margin calculations

QUESTIONS:

  • Does ERPNext handle accrued vendor rebates natively?
  • How to manage “provisional costing” until rebate realization?
  • Best approach for retroactive cost adjustments when rebate is realized?
  • Should I use Landed Cost, or custom scripting, or manual journal entries?

GOAL: Accurate unit costs and margins from purchase moment, not waiting for rebate execution.

Any insights or workarounds appreciated!

posts.name: Talha Butt2508
posts.cooked:
Case 1: Supplier Rebate

  • Purchase Receipt is booked at actual cost:
    • 100 units × $10 = $1,000.
  • When supplier later issues the rebate (say $100):
    • Post a Debit Note (Credit Note from supplier).
    • Book it against Other Income / Supplier Rebate Income account.
    • Stock valuation stays at $10 per unit.

This ensures inventory value doesn’t fluctuate backwards — rebate is treated as income, not cost correction. - This is what we currently do for our Supplier Rebates.

Case 2: Expected vs Actual Landed Cost

  • At purchase time, you may not yet know all clearance, freight, duty costs.
  • You can estimate by adding expected landed cost charges (based on past average %).
  • Once actual clearance bills arrive:
    • Update valuation by adding the actual landing charges.
    • This ensures stock valuation = true landed cost.
